title: Juan Diego, saint (2002)
hook: the Indigenous visionary of Guadalupe canonized almost five centuries later

segments.voice: Yesterday, Sublimis Deus, a pope's letter answering a friar's question. Your line was they are truly human. Whose face did you give back? Today ends the week. Day eight hundred forty.

Early one morning, a man named Juan Diego is walking past a hill called Tepeyac, on his way to Mass. He hears singing, like birds, coming from the top. Then a woman's voice calls him by name, tenderly, in his own language, Nahuatl. He climbs, and finds a lady standing there, her clothes shining like the sun. The account of what follows is called the Nican Mopohua, from its opening words in Nahuatl. Today's word is the man she called: Juan Diego.
screen: `SINGING ON THE HILL.` → `CALLED BY NAME, IN NAHUATL.` → `THE NICAN MOPOHUA.`

segments.voice: First, the request. In the account, the lady says she is the Virgin Mary, and asks for a church to be built on that spot, where she can show her love to all who come. She sends Juan Diego to the bishop in the city to ask for it. Second, the refusal, and what Juan Diego says about himself. The bishop listens politely and sends him away. Juan Diego goes back up the hill and begs her to send someone important instead. In the account he calls himself a little man, a nobody, a tail, a leaf, someone others carry. Send a person of standing, he says; they will be believed. She answers that she has plenty of messengers, and she chooses him. Third, the sign. The bishop asks for proof. On the hilltop, in the cold season, Juan Diego finds flowers blooming, gathers them into his tilma, the rough cloak he wears, and carries them to the bishop. When he opens the cloak, the flowers fall out, and on the cloth is an image of the lady. That cloak hangs in the basilica of Guadalupe in Mexico City. Fourth, the name. Again and again in the account, Mary calls him by tender words for the smallest, youngest child in a family. There's a line in Matthew's Gospel that fits him. In the Douay-Rheims, Jesus thanks his Father, "because thou hast hid these things from the wise and prudent, and hast revealed them to little ones." Pope John Paul the Second declared Juan Diego a saint in Mexico City, at that same basilica. The man who asked to be replaced by someone important became the one remembered.
screen: `A CHURCH ON THE HILL.` · `SEND SOMEONE IMPORTANT.` · `FLOWERS IN A ROUGH CLOAK.` · `HER NAME FOR HIM: THE YOUNGEST.` · then, large: `REVEALED TO LITTLE ONES.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: honor an Indigenous saint. Sit and breathe, and picture Juan Diego on the road with his cloak bundled in his arms, walking toward a bishop who doubted him. Stay with him for a while. If you pray, you can ask for his prayers, or for the prayers of another Indigenous saint you know, such as Kateri Tekakwitha. If you don't, simply honor him in the quiet: a man who thought he was too small, and went anyway. The bell holds the time.
Juan Diego. The Indigenous man who, in the account of Guadalupe, carried flowers in his cloak to a doubting bishop, and was named a saint at the basilica beside that hill. Today's word.

Your line: the little one. This week went from prayer in paint, to a church that has sinned, to two hands almost touching, to remembering honestly, to a man who changed, to people who are truly human, and now to the little one. Today, do one thing you feel too small for. Day eight hundred forty.

howItsDone: Catholics keep Saint Juan Diego's feast in December, just before the feast of Our Lady of Guadalupe; pilgrims come to the basilica in Mexico City to see the tilma, and parishes across the Americas celebrate Guadalupe with Masses, processions and roses.
